dietEvidence.body: The dentition is consistent with carnivory. No gut contents are known; prey choice and hunting method are inferred from skull and postcranial anatomy.

sizeNote: Length and mass are estimates from incomplete material, not measurements of a whole animal.
tagline: A carcharodontosaurid with a triangular hump over the hips and possible quill knobs on the forearm. The hump is bone; the quill interpretation is debated.
summary: Concavenator corcovatus is a carcharodontosaurid from the Las Hoyas locality of Spain, known from a nearly complete articulated skeleton. It has a tall triangular hump over the pelvis formed by elongated neural spines. Possible quill knobs on the ulna have been interpreted as evidence for a feather-like covering, but the identification is contested.

discovery.body: Named by Ortega et al., 2010. The record is known from Las Hoyas, Cuenca. A nearly complete, articulated skeleton from Las Hoyas.

fossilEvidence.title: Stratigraphic and geographic occurrence
fossilEvidence.body: Las Hoyas, Cuenca records the species in the Early Cretaceous. The numeric range used here is ≈130–125 Ma, an occurrence estimate rather than a direct date on every specimen.

fossilEvidence.title: Articulated holotype
fossilEvidence.body: The holotype is a nearly complete, articulated skeleton from Las Hoyas. It preserves the pelvic hump and the ulna, including the structures interpreted as possible quill knobs.

anatomy.title: Preserved anatomy
anatomy.body: The presacral vertebrae form a tall, triangular hump, and the ulna bears a row of bumps interpreted as possible feather attachments.

behaviour.body: The behavioural evidence is skeletal: the pelvic hump and possible ulnar quill knobs are usually interpreted as display structures, but their function is not demonstrated. Social behaviour is unknown.

reconstruction.body: A licensed life reconstruction is assigned to this record and credited in Sources and credits. The species is known from a nearly complete, articulated skeleton from Las Hoyas. The reconstruction is an artist's interpretation of appearance, not a direct observation from the fossil record; preserved integument, where present, is described in the anatomy section, and the soft-tissue outline is otherwise inferred.

confidenceNote: The holotype is exceptionally complete and articulated. The quill-knob interpretation is debated, and the soft tissue of the hump is unknown. The species is known from a single major specimen.
